opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, these are two of the levers I find most exciting right now, and they're complementary.

On distillation, I've been interested in it for a long time. Geoff Hinton, Oriol Vinyals, and I wrote a paper on it about a decade ago. The core insight still holds: a large, capable model's full output distribution carries much more information than a hard label. When the big model says "this is probably a dog, but there's some chance it's a wolf," that structure teaches a smaller model far more efficiently than the raw data alone. So you can train the most capable model you can afford, then distill it into much smaller models that keep a surprising fraction of the capability while being far cheaper and faster to serve. That matters enormously at scale, because most real-world usage needs low latency and low cost, not the absolute frontier on every query.

Inference-time scaling is a different axis. Instead of putting all the compute into training, you let the model spend more compute on a particular problem: reasoning step by step, exploring multiple approaches, checking its own work, using tools. For hard problems like a tricky math proof or a complex coding task, letting the model think longer can give dramatic quality improvements. And it's adaptive. You don't need to think hard about "what's the capital of France," but you might want a lot of thinking on a hard research question.

What's really interesting is how they feed into each other. If a model spends a lot of inference compute and arrives at a really good answer, that output becomes high-quality training signal. You can distill the result of all that thinking back into a model, so next time it gets there faster or with less compute. It's a kind of virtuous loop: inference-time compute expands what's achievable, and distillation compresses those gains into something cheaper.

So I don't think of it as pretraining scale versus inference scale versus distillation. You want all of them, and the interesting engineering question is how to allocate compute across them for the tasks people actually care about.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think of these as two different levers that both let you spend compute in places other than pretraining, and they turn out to be really complementary.

Distillation, to me, is fundamentally about separating the question of "what's the most capable model we can build?" from "what's the model we actually want to serve?" You train a very large model, something that's expensive and slow, and then you use it as a teacher. The student sees the full output distribution from the teacher, not just the one-hot label of what the right next token is, and that soft signal is enormously more informative. A big model that says "this token is 60 percent likely, this other one is 30 percent, these three are plausible" is transferring a lot of structure about the world in every example. So you get a small model that's much better than it would be if you'd just trained it from scratch on the same data. And that matters because most inference in the world should be happening on models that are a lot smaller than the frontier. People want low latency, they want to run things on a phone, they want cheap tokens for a high-volume application. Distillation is how you make the frontier capabilities trickle down into those regimes.

I'd also say distillation gives you a pretty clean way of thinking about an organization's model portfolio. You have a flagship, and then you have a family of smaller models that are really derived from it rather than being independently designed. That's how we've approached Gemini, with the Flash models and the Nano models and so on. Every time the big model gets better, the whole family can get better.

Inference-time scaling is the other axis. For a long time, the dominant view was that all the compute goes into training, and then at inference you do one forward pass per token and that's it. But a lot of problems are genuinely hard in a way where more thinking helps. If you give the model room to reason, explore a few approaches, check its own work, sample multiple candidates and verify them, you can take the same set of weights and get materially better answers. And the nice thing is that it's adjustable. For an easy question, you don't want to spend a lot. For a hard math problem or a complex coding task, you might be happy to spend a thousand times more compute if it gets you a correct answer instead of a wrong one. So you can think of it as a dial, and the right position of the dial depends on the problem and on what the user is willing to wait for and pay for.

Where it gets interesting is the interaction between the two. You can use inference-time scaling on a very large model to produce much higher quality outputs than that model would produce in a single pass, and then distill those outputs back into a model. So the student is effectively learning from a teacher that was allowed to think for a long time. In some sense you're compressing search into weights. And that creates a flywheel: better model, more thinking, better data, distill, better model. I think we're pretty early in understanding how far that loop goes.

From a systems perspective, this also changes what you optimize. If inference-time compute matters a lot, then the cost per token and the latency of serving really start to drive how much capability you can afford to deploy. That pulls on hardware design, on how you do batching and speculative decoding, on how you lay things out across TPUs. So to me the whole thing is of a piece: the algorithmic ideas and the systems work feed each other, and the goal is to get the most useful capability per unit of compute into people's hands.

astra-6.text:
I think of them as complementary. With distillation, you’re trying to take the capabilities of a more expensive model and capture as much of that as possible in a model that’s cheaper to run. That can make a useful level of capability available at much lower latency and cost.

Inference-time scaling asks a different question: for a particular problem, can we get a better answer by spending more computation on it? That might mean exploring several approaches, checking an answer, or revising it when you find a mistake. The important thing is that the extra computation has to be productive. Generating more tokens doesn’t automatically make an answer better.

There’s a nice connection between the two. If additional computation lets you produce better solutions, you can use those solutions to help train a model that gets to a good answer more directly. So you can spend computation to discover better behavior, then distill some of that behavior into a more efficient model.

Ultimately, you’d like the system to allocate effort according to the problem. A straightforward question should get a quick answer. A difficult problem should get more work, provided that work actually improves the result.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of those as complementary approaches. With distillation, you’re trying to take capabilities you’ve developed in a larger, more expensive model and make them available in a smaller, more efficient one. That can make a big difference in how broadly you can deploy those capabilities, particularly when latency and cost matter.

Inference-time scaling asks a different question: for a particular problem, can you get a better answer by spending more computation before you respond? You might explore several possible solutions, check them, and refine the most promising one. That’s particularly useful for problems where checking an answer is easier than producing it in the first place.

And there’s a nice connection between the two. If additional inference-time computation produces better solutions, those solutions can become training examples. You can then distill some of that improvement into a model that produces good answers more directly. So you have this cycle of spending computation to discover better behavior, then using training to make that behavior cheaper.

The interesting question is how to allocate that computation. A straightforward question probably doesn’t need a lot of deliberation. A difficult reasoning problem might benefit substantially. You’d like the system to learn when that extra effort is actually useful.
